text:
Ray Dalio says investors mistake great technology for a great investment in a bubble and compares the AI boom with the innovations of the 1920s

“A lot of people think a bubble is whether the price gets beyond that which can come from the present value of future cash flows, and that’s not it, because what happens is you don’t know the future cash flows for decades, let’s say, if you take the present value.

“In any case, even those with good financial cash flows have had bubbles. So you could see the 1920s bubbles, and then you have the collapses. Even if they work out in the long run, you have the bubble bursting.

“The bubble, the mechanics of it, is that people mistake a great new technology for a great investment.

“In the ’20s, imagine what that was like. That was the first time you had electricity in houses, so you had lighting and you had refrigeration. You had movies, you had radio, you had cars, you had airplanes—all of this new technology coming on. It would be more apparent than anything we’ve seen even with AI.”

• Traditional Servers: Unit shipments declined despite 235% revenue growth, driven by higher pricing and richer configurations. Servers priced below $3,000, previously accounting for 20% of units but just 2% of revenue, have virtually disappeared. 

• Agentic AI: The fastest-growing segment of Dell's traditional server business for four consecutive quarters, with AI-oriented CPU servers commanding significantly higher selling prices. 

• AI Backlog: Orders span nearly 100 data center sites globally, roughly evenly split between U.S. and international locations. Management reports no customer order rescheduling to date. 

• Customer Financing: Financing receivables increased by only ~$500M QoQ despite $22B in quarterly AI shipments. Dell reviews underlying customer contracts and projected weekly cash inflows. 

• Server Consolidation: Dell says its 17G servers can replace approximately seven older servers, while 18G systems can replace 12–14 in certain configurations.

• 2027 Outlook: Management expects the AI demand-supply gap to widen further in 2027, projects ~87x token growth by the end of the decade and is tracking over 200 GW of data center and power infrastructure projects.

Steve Eisman reveals he shorted roughly half his Nvidia holding against his long position before Jensen was reinstated, and says he hedged much of his technology portfolio months ago

Steven Bartlett: “What are you investing in in this moment? I’ve been thinking a lot about this.”

Steve Eisman: “I had a lot of the technology companies in my portfolio, and about four months or so, I shorted most of them against the box to reduce my risk.”

Steven Bartlett: “You shorted most of them against the box? What does that mean?”

Steve Eisman: “Let’s say I own 100 shares of Nvidia, just make up a number, and I’ve owned it for a very long time. And I’m nervous. The problem is, if I sell my Nvidia, I’ve got to pay massive taxes on the gain. And I don’t want to do that, unless I’m so freaked out that I’ll do it anyway. You’re talking about 30%, 35% taxes. It’s a lot.

“So what you can do for a time, you can’t do it forever, is I can short 50 shares or 75 shares or even 100 shares of Nvidia. So now my Nvidia exposure is a lot lower.

“If I were to do that today, I’d have to cover the entire position at the end of January. That’s just the way the tax rules work. But during that period, I wouldn’t have any real exposure to Nvidia. That’s what I did.”

Steven Bartlett: “So you’re shorting Nvidia?”

Steve Eisman: “Well, I’m long it, and I shorted like half of my position.”
